claims: Medicine-ball protocols define projection direction and movement sequence explicitly.
Forward bilateral chest projection and transverse rotational projection are separate identities, not difficulty or proficiency levels.
Medicine-ball throws require exact stance, countermovement, projection, target, release, contacts, and reset taxonomy.
Declare forward versus transverse projection and bilateral versus side-specific sequencing.
Rotational throwing performance relates to trunk rotator strength, while full-body throws also use lower-body drive and upper-limb release.
Declare foot, ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, spine, scapulothoracic, shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand roles.
Dynamic medicine-ball throws use a declared countermovement to create momentum before release.
Observe ball start, lower-body preload, ground-up sequence, trunk control, projection plane, release, foot contacts, finish, and reset.
Ball load and standing protocol affect measured throwing velocity.
Score exact variants on exercise complexity and physical difficulty and derive overall difficulty as their maximum; no exercise skill level is assigned.
Medicine-ball output can be quantified and declines when effort or technique changes.
Track ball mass, high-intent throws, output loss, shoulder and elbow response, trunk control, contact or catch load, and recovery.
ACE requires a prepared partner or suitable wall or rebounder, target distance, stable stance, and clear intent.
Declare ball type and mass, wall or partner behavior, target, release lane, return and catch policy, traction, clearance, traffic, retrieval, and coach sightline.
Explosive medicine-ball work should preserve power rather than become fatigue conditioning.
Use short sets, full reset, and enough rest to preserve ball speed, projection, target accuracy, posture, contacts, and safe retrieval.
The U.S. Marine Corps demonstration identifies a medicine-ball chest throw against a wall as an upper-body power task.
Instructions must name exact stance, ball start, countermovement, projection, target, foot contacts, release, return or retrieval, reset, and stop signal.
Partner and wall throws require target readiness and force-aware catching.
Stop for pain or neurologic symptoms, loss of balance, spinal compensation, mistimed release, unsafe foot contacts, damaged ball, occupied lane, unsafe rebound or partner, or output loss.
Medicine-ball throws can serve as standardized power tasks when protocol is controlled.
Use early and fresh for power expression; hold mass and variant constant for comparison and do not use maximal throws as conditioning filler.
Athlete support should show direction, target, ball specification, contacts, cue, reset, and stop signal.
Offer a lighter or softer ball, smaller countermovement, lower-intent rehearsal, fewer attempts, longer rest, high-contrast target, and nonvideo instruction.
Reliable power testing requires a standardized throw protocol.
Expose projection, side, ball mass, target, contacts, attempt count, rest, output measure, observation angle, invalid-attempt rule, return control, and lane shutdown.
Wall or trained-partner targets can provide a visible forward target when logistics permit.
Offer lighter or softer balls, smaller preload, no jump, shorter range, fewer repetitions, longer reset, high-contrast target, plain text, and an appropriate nonthrow substitute.
Projection direction and release path define separate throw tasks.
Ball mass, exact distance, and measurement are annotations; rotation, overhead, scoop, slam, vertical, chest, and backward projections require explicit identity review.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

The stored card declares quadriceps, gluteal, pectoral, triceps, shoulder and bilateral dip-and-drive actions toward a wall, supporting a forward chest projection rather than rotation.
The explicit identity is a bilateral countermovement medicine-ball chest pass to a forward target.

assessmentSummary.identity: A bilateral two-hand medicine-ball chest pass projected forward from the chest toward an inspected wall, trained partner, or open release lane; stationary, shallow-countermovement, and squat-countermovement starts are exact variants.
currentCardFindings: The broader Medicine Ball Chest Pass definition is the stable forward two-hand projection identity.

The consolidated countermovement source declares coordinated dip-and-drive, pectoral and triceps contribution, elbow extension, and a wall target; those dimensions belong on exact preload variants rather than a separate definition.
Generic legacy baselines remain archived because they omit stance, preload, ball, target, contacts, return, dose, and stop contract.

claims: A standing rotational wall toss uses side-on orientation and ground-up transverse force transfer.
The explicit identity is a side-specific countermovement rotational medicine-ball throw, distinct from forward bilateral chest projection.

assessmentSummary.identity: A side-on, side-specific two-hand medicine-ball wall throw using a declared rotational countermovement, ground-up hip-pelvis-trunk sequence, transverse release, controlled finish, and full reset.
currentCardFindings: The legacy card already declares rotational projection, hip and thoracic rotation, shoulder horizontal action, and ground-up force transfer.
It lacks exact stance, pivot, ball start, wall target, return, side, dose, and difficulty dimensions.
Its transverse projection is a deterministic boundary from the generic card's forward chest action.
